arguments.conclusion: The increase in the Treasury General Account during the shutdown reduces liquidity in the financial system, contributing to market volatility.

arguments.premise_synthesis: The Treasury General Account has risen to approximately $940 billion, overshooting its $850 billion target, because the government continues to collect taxes and borrow but is not spending discretionary funds due to the shutdown. Since the TGA is held outside the banking system, each dollar added reduces liquidity in the financial system. Financial institutions' usage of the Federal Reserve's repo facility has spiked, indicating liquidity stress.
arguments.conclusion_supported: The immediate effect of the government shutdown on monetary liquidity is a drain via the TGA that directly contributes to stock market volatility.

arguments.premise_synthesis: When the shutdown ends, all funds that were not spent will be released into the economy, effectively reversing the liquidity drain. The Treasury itself does not perform quantitative easing or tightening; only the Federal Reserve does such operations, so the government's accumulation does not permanently alter liquidity conditions.
arguments.conclusion_supported: While the TGA drain causes temporary stress, the long-term effect on monetary policy and liquidity conditions is neutral because the withheld spending will eventually be injected back into the financial system.
